name: LOVE Protocol
analogy: Two neighbors share a garden. Forgive an accidental broken tool, but set boundaries if one neighbor repeatedly takes the harvest.
problem: When should an agent cooperate, punish or forgive in repeated encounters?
mechanism: The archived design describes an eight-action trust window, tolerance for occasional defections and a conditional forgiveness branch. Actions are cooperate or defect. Track each player’s payoff and cooperation separately; a policy can improve one while harming the other.
formula: c = N(C) / N; π = Σ rₜ / N
variables: Total actions or rounds in the relevant measure
Mean payoff per round, in game units
example: Teaching example, not a LOVE run: payoffs 3, 3, 0, 5 give π = 11 / 4 = 2.75 game units. If 3 of 4 actions cooperate, c = 75%. The two measures answer different questions.
achieved: The original website documents a synthetic cooperation/payoff trade-off: more cooperation accompanied lower individual payoff. Its exact outputs have not been reproduced for this release.
unverified: Original synthetic scripts, seeds and raw outputs are absent here. The newer unfavorable evolutionary outcome is user-reported and awaits original-source inspection and independent reruns.
failure: An opponent can exploit predictable forgiveness. Cooperation is not an evolutionary stability proof.
value: Potentially fewer disputes and failed partnerships. Measure avoided incident cost minus monitoring, concessions and implementation costs; never convert game points directly to dollars.
experiment: Obtain the original archive; freeze policies, payoff matrix and noise; run matched seeds against cooperative, retaliating and exploitative opponents, including invasion tests.
baseline: Tit-for-Tat, always defect and a strong forgiving baseline, with identical noise and opponents.
metric: Paired mean payoff, cooperation fraction, worst-opponent loss and uncertainty across seeds.
criterion: Reject an advantage claim if the confidence interval for payoff improvement includes zero or adversarial losses exceed a preregistered safety limit.
steps: Specify actions, payoff rules and forgiveness exactly.
Replay equal-length encounters with matched random seeds.
Compare cooperation, individual payoff and exploitability separately.

name: Redemption Amplifier
analogy: A library restores borrowing privileges after reliable behavior, while preventing someone from repeatedly cheating and resetting their record.
problem: How much evidence should restore trust after a violation?
mechanism: A candidate rule subtracts a severity penalty from a bounded trust score, then rewards verified reliable actions. A restoration multiplier is a tunable hypothesis, not a proven fairness mechanism.
formula: T′ = min(1, max(0, T − s + k·r))
variables: Trust score before and after a review (0–1)
Verified recovery evidence in score units
example: Illustrative rule: T = 0.4, s = 0.2, k = 1.5 and r = 0.1 give T′ = 0.35. A larger multiplier restores privileges faster but can also help repeat offenders.
achieved: The archive describes a multiplier concept and a separate simplified ablation claim. They must not be treated as the same tested algorithm.
unverified: No supplied run establishes that the multiplier reduces exploitation or improves fairness. The toy rule here only explains the mechanism.
failure: Alternating misconduct and minimum recovery can become a profitable strategy.
value: Compare avoided false exclusions against repeat fraud, review labor and reinstatement costs. Recovery speed alone is not economic success.
experiment: Freeze this candidate rule and simulate repeated offenders alongside genuinely reformed agents; vary multiplier and observation error.
baseline: Permanent exclusion, fixed probation and recovery without amplification.
metric: Repeat-offense loss, false exclusion rate and median time to safe restoration.
criterion: Reject if faster recovery raises total loss or false exclusion beyond a declared tolerance.
steps: Define the violation and what counts as recovery evidence.
Apply bounded penalties and controlled restoration.
Test whether repeated cheating becomes more attractive.
sourceNote: Original description is available; executable project research and raw outputs are not supplied in this repository. Website teaching models are separate implementations.

name: BioSynth.AI
analogy: A librarian gathers evidence, a scientist proposes an explanation and a skeptic checks it. They all leave notes you can inspect.
problem: Can automated research produce more supported answers per hour?
mechanism: Keep a claim ledger with source passages, alternative explanations and executable checks. A verifier marks unsupported claims and a human resolves conflicts before publication.
formula: q = S / C; cost_correct = K / V
variables: Total research and review cost in dollars
example: If 18 of 20 checked claims are supported, q = 90%. If a workflow costs $60 and produces 15 accepted answers, cost_correct = $4. Neither number is a measured BioSynth result.
achieved: This repository implements an educational website and arithmetic demos. The earlier site describes recovered research components, but does not include them.
unverified: An end-to-end autonomous research engine and a measured accuracy advantage are not established by this checkout.
failure: Agents can repeat the same unsupported claim; many citations can still fail to support the conclusion.
value: Measure cost per accepted answer, including source retrieval, inference, correction and reviewer time. Count work only after verification.
experiment: Create a frozen set of answerable research questions and source snapshots; blind reviewers to the workflow used.
baseline: One model with retrieval and the same time, sources and reviewer budget.
metric: Source support, correct answers, correction minutes and full dollars per accepted answer.
criterion: Reject superiority if quality does not improve at equal total cost, or if hidden review labor explains the gain.
steps: Attach every factual claim to a source passage.
Generate a rival explanation and a check that could distinguish it.
Publish accepted results with unresolved claims still visible.
sourceNote: Original description is available; executable project research and raw outputs are not supplied in this repository. Website teaching models are separate implementations.

name: APEX
analogy: A coach chooses the best training plan that fits the budget, schedule and safety rules.
problem: Which feasible decision offers the most value under real constraints?
mechanism: Define a measurable objective, enumerate feasible decisions and choose the highest-value one. Hard limits constrain the choice; arbitrary weighted scores require explicit justification.
formula: maxₓ V(x), subject to C(x) ≤ B and H(x) ≤ L
variables: A candidate decision or resource allocation
Value of the decision in declared units
Resource usage and its hard limit
example: Plan A costs $80 and has modeled benefit $120; plan B costs $110 and benefit $170. With budget B = $100, only A is feasible. Its modeled net is $40, not the $60 of infeasible B.
achieved: A conceptual optimization framework is described. Constrained optimization is established mathematics; naming a framework does not establish a new theorem.
unverified: No supplied comparative benchmark shows APEX beats existing decision rules.
failure: Incorrect objectives optimize the wrong thing; inconsistent units make weighted rankings meaningless.
value: Incremental realized net value relative to the best feasible alternative, including decision and oversight costs.
experiment: Choose one scheduling or procurement dataset; preregister objective and constraints, then compare on held-out cases.
baseline: Existing practice, a simple greedy rule and a conventional optimization solver.
metric: Feasible net value, constraint violations and decision time.
criterion: Reject if a simpler baseline matches value at lower cost or any hard safety constraint is violated.
steps: Choose the outcome and units before scoring candidates.
Remove decisions that violate budget or safety limits.
Compare the best feasible decision with a simple baseline.
sourceNote: Original description is available; executable project research and raw outputs are not supplied in this repository. Website teaching models are separate implementations.

priorArt.label: Background: Boyd & Vandenberghe, Convex Optimization (2004)
priorArt.note: Author-hosted textbook on constrained convex optimization. Background mathematics; not evidence that APEX is superior or that every APEX problem is convex.

name: FORGE
analogy: A bridge closure can send traffic pressure through many neighborhoods. A supplier disruption can spread through a company network.
problem: Where might semiconductor supply-chain disruption create indirect exposure?
mechanism: A directed graph connects pressure sources to exposed targets. Normalize incoming edge weights into matrix P, inject scenario b and iterate a damped propagation rule. Scores are illustrative unsigned exposures.
variables: Vector of illustrative exposure scores at iteration t
Scenario source vector, in score units
Nonnegative matrix with every row sum at most 1
example: Two-node toy: b = (1, 0), d = 0.5 and P₂₁ = 0.8, with all other entries zero. The fixed point is x₁ = 0.5 and x₂ = 0.2. A score of 0.2 is neither 20% loss nor a 20% probability.
achieved: Public MODEL.md was inspected. It specifies normalization, convergence bounds and the distinction between relationship evidence and assumed coefficients.
unverified: The external engine was not executed in this release. Edge weights are not calibrated loss estimates or validated stock forecasts.
failure: A disclosed supplier relationship does not reveal dependence, substitution or inventory buffers.
value: Prioritize due diligence and resilience analysis. Measure whether scenario-guided decisions reduce disruption costs compared with ordinary review.
experiment: Freeze pre-event graphs and compare exposure rankings around documented disruptions, without using facts published after each event.
baseline: Direct-supplier-only exposure and simple industry concentration rankings.
metric: Rank calibration and decision usefulness across held-out historical events.
criterion: Reject predictive claims if rankings fail to improve on the direct-only baseline; do not infer dollar losses without calibration.
steps: Document each relationship and separate assumed weights.
Propagate a declared disruption through a bounded network.
Check sensitivity and compare historical event rankings.
sourceNote: Public source inspected on 2026-10-29. Source availability is not independent reproduction or field validation.

name: Q-Branch Purchasing
analogy: A $75 item arriving after your trip can cost more in lost use than a $90 item ready today.
problem: How should price, delivery time and uncertainty influence a purchase?
mechanism: Add acquisition costs to the opportunity cost of waiting. Treat delivery probability as an assumption to calibrate. Missing arrival information is unknown risk, never evidence of safe delivery.
formula: C = P + S + T + R + V + d·u
variables: Expected repair and pickup travel cost ($)
example: With other costs set to zero, shipped option costs $75 + 5 days × $4/day = $95. Local pickup costs $90 + 0 = $90. Local has $5 lower modeled economic cost, not $5 proven cash savings.
achieved: Public Python source was inspected: it implements acquisition cost and a delivery-window assumption.
unverified: Actual purchasing improvements and delivery calibration remain unverified. The source defaults unknown late risk to zero; users must not interpret that as certainty.
failure: Assumed delivery windows and daily value can dominate the ranking. A point estimate hides uncertainty.
value: Compare missed deadlines, expediting, repair costs and user-valued waiting against the price-only choice.
experiment: Collect de-identified purchases with predicted and actual arrival dates; evaluate rankings and deadline probabilities.
baseline: Lowest posted price and a simple deadline-screened price rule.
metric: Total observed cost, deadline misses and probability calibration.
criterion: Reject if adjusted choices do not reduce held-out cost or deadline misses relative to simple rules.
steps: List all cash costs and the value of earlier use.
Estimate arrival uncertainty without filling unknowns with zero.
Compare total economic cost and audit actual outcomes.
sourceNote: Public source inspected on 2026-10-29. Source availability is not independent reproduction or field validation.

name: OTSA
analogy: An investing GPS must include tolls, rough roads and taxes when comparing routes.
problem: Can an investment policy improve after-cost, after-tax outcomes at comparable risk?
mechanism: Proposed regime estimation and portfolio rules select trades under risk and tax-lot constraints. Tax-aware means keeping track of the acquisition cost and holding period of each lot; no current tax rate is assumed here.
variables: Slippage: execution cost relative to the assumed price ($)
Modeled tax cost ($), supplied as a scenario
example: Illustrative arithmetic: $1,000 gross gain − $80 fees − $70 execution cost − $200 hypothetical tax = $650 net gain. This says nothing about OTSA profitability or current tax treatment.
achieved: An investment research design is described in the archive. No verified trading record is supplied.
unverified: Profitability, generalization, tax correctness and out-of-sample performance are unverified.
failure: Future information leakage, repeated tuning and unrealistic fills can create fictional backtest profits.
value: Compare after-cost, after-tax outcomes and drawdowns at matched risk. Include data, compute, turnover and review costs.
experiment: Freeze strategy and point-in-time dataset; retain a genuinely untouched test interval and run a cost-sensitive walk-forward evaluation.
baseline: Low-turnover benchmark portfolio under the same cost and tax assumptions.
metric: Net return, drawdown, turnover, benchmark difference and uncertainty.
criterion: Reject superiority if held-out advantage disappears under realistic cost sensitivity or cannot survive correction for repeated trials.
steps: Freeze the strategy before viewing the evaluation period.
Apply fees, execution frictions and declared tax assumptions.
Compare net results at similar risk and report losing periods.
sourceNote: Original description is available; executable project research and raw outputs are not supplied in this repository. Website teaching models are separate implementations.

name: Quantum-Inspired Q-Branch
analogy: A detective keeps several explanations open and changes their confidence when new evidence arrives.
problem: Can considering competing hypotheses improve decisions under uncertainty?
mechanism: Generate rival explanations, collect distinguishing evidence and update beliefs. This lesson uses ordinary Bayesian probability on classical hardware; it does not implement quantum computation.
example: With prior p = 0.4, a = 0.8 and b = 0.2, the updated probability is 0.32 / 0.44 ≈ 72.7%. These are assumed probabilities, not measured model confidence.
achieved: A conceptual architecture is described; this release provides a classical probability teaching calculator.
unverified: No quantum speedup, quantum mechanism or accuracy advantage over strong classical methods is established.
failure: Correlated branches repeat mistakes; guessed likelihoods can create false confidence.
value: Value equals avoided decision loss minus additional inference and review cost, measured at matched budgets.
experiment: Test a frozen set of verifiable tasks using single-path and multi-hypothesis methods at equal total inference and review budgets.
baseline: Single-path reasoning and a strong classical search or planning baseline.
metric: Correct answers per dollar, calibration and abstention quality.
criterion: Reject if improvements vanish at equal budget or confidence becomes less calibrated.
steps: Keep distinct explanations and explicit initial probabilities.
Seek evidence that would differ under those explanations.
Update confidence and retain unresolved uncertainty.
sourceNote: Original description is available; executable project research and raw outputs are not supplied in this repository. Website teaching models are separate implementations.

priorArt.label: Background: Thomas Bayes, An Essay… (1763)
priorArt.note: University-hosted transcription of the historical primary essay on inverse probability. Historical background; not a validation of Q-Branch or its assumed likelihoods.

name: Multi-Agent Evolution
analogy: A village changes when successful behaviors spread, even if one friendly pair gets along well.
problem: Which strategies survive competition, mutation and invasion?
mechanism: Track strategy shares over generations. The teaching demo uses two-strategy discrete replicator selection: shares rise when expected payoff exceeds the population average. It is not a LOVE experiment.
variables: Share of strategy A before and after selection
A expected payoff, 4p in this toy coordination game
Assumed game payoffs, not measured economic values
example: At p = 0.6, f_A = 2.4 and f_B = 3. Average payoff is 2.76; p′ = 1.44 / 2.76 ≈ 0.522. A shrinks. It grows only above p = 0.75 under these specific rules.
achieved: This release implements a deterministic teaching recurrence. Archived historical population claims have not been independently reproduced.
unverified: The described newer unfavorable LOVE study requires the original repository, algorithm versions, seeds and outputs before its result can be verified.
failure: Changing payoff rules, mutation or update mechanics changes the outcome. A curated opponent panel cannot establish invasion resistance.
value: Explore the durability of cooperative institutions. Game payoffs remain game units; an operational value claim needs a separate field comparison.
experiment: Obtain original LOVE evolution materials; preregister mixed populations, rare-invader tests, selection rules, noise and seed panels.
baseline: Always defect, Tit-for-Tat and forgiving competitors under the identical selection process.
metric: Invasion success, fixation frequency, population payoff and cooperation over seeds.
criterion: Reject stability if a rare competitor reliably invades across the preregistered conditions.
steps: Specify the population, payoff matrix and selection rule.
Run invasion and mutation conditions across many seeds.
Separate pairwise success from population survival.
sourceNote: Original description is available; executable project research and raw outputs are not supplied in this repository. Website teaching models are separate implementations.

priorArt.label: Background: Taylor & Jonker, Evolutionary stable strategies and game dynamics (1978)
priorArt.note: Original evolutionary game-dynamics paper. Background theory; the site’s discrete teaching recurrence is not a reproduction of that paper or of LOVE. Publisher access may be restricted.

name: Dignity Optimization
analogy: A school cannot improve average scores by excluding children who need help. Rights constrain the decision.
problem: How can resource allocation improve outcomes while respecting rights?
mechanism: Optimize a declared service outcome subject to justified minimum access, consent and safety constraints. Human dignity is a boundary on permissible decisions, not a scalar measure of human worth.
formula: max Σ uᵢxᵢ, subject to Σ cᵢxᵢ ≤ B and xᵢ ≥ mᵢ
variables: Service units allocated to group i
Declared service outcome per unit, not human worth
example: Two groups need at least 3 sessions each. At $10 a session and budget $80, the first 6 sessions cost $60, leaving $20 for 2 additional sessions. The minimum comes from a rights process, not the equation.
achieved: A rights-constrained allocation proposal is documented. No ethical or clinical validation is supplied.
unverified: Consent, proxy fairness and real distributive effects need participatory evaluation before deployment.
failure: Unjustified minimums or biased outcome measures can encode discrimination in a precise-looking model.
value: Compare service outcomes and budget use while preserving rights. Do not assign a dollar price to dignity.
experiment: Co-design constraints with affected groups; test adversarial cases, infeasible budgets and disparate access before any pilot.
baseline: Current allocation and a rights-preserving rule with no optimization.
metric: Access gaps, rights violations, service outcomes and feasibility.
criterion: Reject any policy violating agreed rights; when the budget is infeasible, report infeasibility rather than silently relaxing rights.
steps: Agree on rights and minimum access with affected people.
Check whether the budget can satisfy those constraints.
Compare outcomes only among ethically feasible options.
sourceNote: Original description is available; executable project research and raw outputs are not supplied in this repository. Website teaching models are separate implementations.

name: Autonomous AI Systems
analogy: A restaurant team can divide jobs well, but making four people check every sandwich may cost more than it saves.
problem: When do orchestration and local inference improve business workflow quality and cost?
mechanism: Route tasks among models, retrieval and tools; validate outputs and require authorized human approval before consequential actions. Local inference runs a model on organization-controlled hardware, with hardware and staffing costs included.
variables: Full cost per accepted correct task ($)
example: For an assumed batch: $30 hardware + $5 energy + $15 maintenance + $50 review = $100. If 20 tasks pass review, k = $5 per correct task. Free model weights do not make the workflow free.
achieved: An orchestration architecture is described. This site runs locally in the browser and does not call AI services.
unverified: Company-wide deployment, privacy properties of an actual system and superiority of local or multi-agent inference are not verified.
failure: Errors propagate across tools; broad permissions or weak retrieval controls can expose data despite local inference.
value: Compare correct tasks per total dollar, latency and oversight load. Include hardware utilization and amortization when comparing local and hosted models.
experiment: Use synthetic documents and a fixed task suite; compare single-model, routed-agent and human-assisted workflows with identical acceptance criteria.
baseline: A single capable model plus retrieval and ordinary workflow automation.
metric: Accepted completions, error severity, human correction time, latency and full cost.
criterion: Reject claimed efficiency if review cost or serious error rates offset the throughput gain.
steps: Classify tasks, permissions and where information may flow.
Route to a model and verify output before tool execution.
Measure accepted work and full lifecycle cost.
sourceNote: Original description is available; executable project research and raw outputs are not supplied in this repository. Website teaching models are separate implementations.

name: Freight RFQ Optimization
analogy: A careful assistant copies carrier quotes into the same comparison sheet, flags uncertain numbers and waits for the decision-maker to approve.
problem: Can quotations be processed faster without changing approval rights?
mechanism: Extract fields from email or PDF into one master Excel workbook. Logistics checks ambiguous fields and sends the comparison to the business unit. The business unit chooses; logistics books only after a recorded approval.
formula: H = q·12·(m − a)/60; G = H·w; R = G·f; N₁ = R − O − D
variables: Manual and automated human minutes per quotation
Annual released labor hours; can be negative
Gross annual capacity value ($), not cash savings
Annual realized value ($), still an assumption until measured
Annual operating and one-time development cost ($)
example: 400 monthly quotes, 15 → 4 human minutes, $35/hour and 50% realization yield 880 hours, $30,800 gross capacity and $15,400 realized value. Subtract $4,800 operating and $12,000 build cost: first-year net = −$1,400.
achieved: Workflow design and an interactive capacity calculator are implemented in this educational release. No freight extraction engine or production booking system is included.
unverified: Extraction accuracy, operational adoption, hours saved and actual cash savings have not been established by a measured pilot.
failure: Wrong units, currencies, duplicate quotes or unapproved bookings can erase all time savings.
value: Released capacity may support more work. Cash savings require evidence of avoided spending, overtime or hiring. Apply a disclosed realization fraction and count every cost.
experiment: Use de-identified or synthetic quotations; time manual and assisted handling on matched cases and audit every field and approval transition.
baseline: The existing one-master-workbook process with the same business-unit approval requirement.
metric: Human minutes per quote, exact field accuracy, corrections, approval completeness and realized cost changes.
criterion: Reject deployment if critical-field accuracy or approval compliance is below the agreed threshold, even when average processing is faster.
steps: Extract and flag uncertain fields in the existing master workbook.
Have logistics review and the business unit approve a carrier.
Book only after approval; log time, corrections and outcomes.
